The question of whether identical twins are genetically identical is a matter of conflicting research outcomes. Traditional sources assert that identical twins are genetically identical: d1 states "Identical twins share the same genetic information," d8 (University of Utah Genetics) holds that "identical twins develop from a single fertilized egg, they have the same genome," d12 (Britannica) describes them as "genetically identical," and d14 (PBS/NOVA) explicitly teaches that "identical twins are genetically identical, while fraternal twins are only as genetically similar as typical siblings are." Similarly, d15 (Oxford academic journal) notes that "MZ twins have the same chromosomal DNA sequence, except for very small errors of DNA replication after the four to eight cell zygote stage," and d13 refers to "genetically identical twin-pairs" in Alzheimer's research.

However, newer research directly contradicts this view. d3 (Science News) reports that "on average, identical twins differ by 5.2 genetic changes," with some pairs differing by more than 100 changes, based on a study of 381 twin pairs published in Nature Genetics. d9 (The Scientist) confirms that "identical twins are not as identical as previously assumed," accumulating genetic variation from the earliest stages of development. d11 (Live Science) states plainly that "identical twins don't share 100% of their DNA," and d7 (Healthline) cites a 2021 study estimating that "15 percent of identical twin pairs may have one member that exhibits significant genetic variation from their twin." d4 (Science Daily) reports that researchers at the University of Western Ontario "demonstrated that the monozygotic twins are not genetically identical," and d6 reports forensic discovery of five SNP differences between twin siblings. d2 (Genome Research) takes a middle position, describing identical twins as "nearly genetically identical" while emphasizing epigenetic differences.

In summary, while the traditional and widely taught view holds that identical twins are genetically identical, a growing body of peer-reviewed research [d3, d4, d9, d11] demonstrates that most identical twin pairs accumulate at least some genetic differences early in embryonic development, meaning they are not strictly genetically identical in all cases.
